The campaign's hidden layer (the DM's prep; the player never sees it; the truth comes out through clues, nobody explains all of it):
The truth: Caravans vanish between Beregost and Nashkel. Bandits are not taking them. Bills of lading, sealed in Beregost, send the wagons onto the Cloakwood spur, where a Zhentarim cell trading as 'Ashby & Corve' takes the iron and the men for the reopened Cloakwood mine. The cell's purpose is to make the Trade Way look ungovernable, so that the Council will grant the Zhentarim the right to collect tolls. Captain Halvard Roe of the Flaming Fist pays them and protects them, because he will take a share of those tolls. Aubrey Vallow, Hesper's late husband and a notary, was paid to seal the false bills. He lost his nerve and kept true copies with the real names. He locked them in a coffer under a stolen Lathanderite oath-seal and hid it as a moneylender's pledge, where no one would look. He died 'falling' on the temple steps last winter. The pledge lapses at sundown today, and the cell has bought the right to it. Hesper knows only that the coffer frightened him. Thole knows only the money. Ashby knows only his orders. The temple knows only that its seal is missing.
Factions and their hidden aims:
- The Zhentarim (the 'Ashby & Corve' cell): Keep the Way bleeding until the Council grants the toll right, then 'rescue' it. They are buying Aubrey's forfeited coffer through Thole so they can destroy it unopened, and they have a hired boy watching Hesper's lane in case she holds other copies.
- The Flaming Fist: Most of the Fist knows nothing; it is short of men and blames gnolls. Captain Halvard Roe sits on the toll question in the Gate, files reports that clear the cell, and takes their gold. If his name surfaces he will call it a Zhentarim forgery and send men to bury it.
- The Song of the Morning (temple of Lathander): The temple is Beregost's real authority and its court of contracts. Its archive has listed four dawn-witness seals as lost for ninety years. It wants them back quietly and would claim the coffer as temple property. It would also prefer that no one learn a temple healer was paid to overlook bruises on Aubrey's throat.
- The smiths of Beregost (Thunderhammer and the lesser forges): They are filling large advance-paid orders for mine-picks, chain and spearheads from Ashby & Corve. They suspect where the goods go and do not want to know. Their one aim is to keep the orders coming without being tied to the vanished caravans.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Aubrey Vallow did not die of the fall. The temple healer who laid him out saw finger-marks on his throat. A donation to the temple came the same week, and she wrote 'a fall'.
- Gaspar Thole's pledge book records the coffer as pledged by Aubrey eight months ago for one hundred and twenty gold, redeemable until sundown of this day. Aubrey paid him twenty gold more 'for silence and the full term'.
- Aubrey's pledge has a clause: the coffer may be redeemed by 'the bearer of my ticket or my lawful heir producing it'. The ticket is not in his papers. He left it, folded, with Sister Maudra Kell of the temple archive, 'for my widow, if it comes to it'.
- 'Ashby & Corve' has no house in Baldur's Gate and no letter of credit at the Counting House. Its notes are drawn on a banker in Scornubel, and that banker has no other clients on the Coast.
- At least three of the vanished caravans carried bills of lading sealed in Beregost and routed 'by the Cloakwood spur, for the ford'. No caravan master who knows the Way would take that road in that season.
- The Thunderhammer smithy's order book shows two hundred mine-picks and forty sets of shackle-chain paid in advance by Ashby & Corve. No mine near Beregost has admitted to buying them.
- Captain Halvard Roe of the Flaming Fist signed a report blaming 'gnoll bands' for the second caravan two days before anyone found the wagons.
- The boy watching Hesper's lane is Wat Ferrow, a stable lad at the Red Sheaf. Ashby pays him a silver a day to report who calls on her. He knows nothing beyond the coin and the description he was given.
- Thole is afraid of Ashby and would rather not sell to him. He will not refuse outright, but he would take any refusal that the town could not blame on him.
Clocks:
- clock_pledge_forfeit: The day runs down toward sundown, when Thole's pledge lapses and the coffer passes to Ashby (segments 6; when full: At sundown Thole hands the coffer to Ashby. Ashby rides out on the Cloakwood road with two hired blades and means to burn the coffer unopened at the first ford.)
- clock_cell_attention: The cell notices who is working for Hesper Vallow (segments 6; when full: Ashby concludes Hesper has copies or hired help. Her house is broken into that night, and the party is named to the cell as a problem.)
- clock_next_caravan: A caravan forms at Feldepost's Inn with a bill of lading routed by the Cloakwood spur (segments 8; when full: The caravan leaves Beregost and vanishes on the Way, guards and all. A fourth set of empty wagons is left for the Fist to blame on gnolls.)
The wonder: The wax on Aubrey's iron coffer is pale gold and still faintly warm to the touch, and it is not his notary's mark. It shows a sun-disc split by an upright key, with a line of tiny dawn-script letters around the rim. Any light brought near it seems to lean toward it. Its history: It is one of four dawn-witness seals that the archivists of the Song of the Morning made about two centuries ago to witness oaths between merchant houses. A name is spoken into the wax as it is set. Only that hand can break it; any other hand makes the wax flare and burn the contents to ash. The archive has listed all four as lost in a fire ninety years ago. Aubrey had one, which means at least one was taken out before the fire, or by someone using it. The open question: Whose name did Aubrey speak into the wax? Hesper's, his own dead hand, or someone the party has not met? And where are the other three seals, and what are they witnessing now?
Clues to the truth:
- Thole's pledge book and counting-room, at his house on the main street: the coffer's entry, the sundown term, the twenty gold 'for silence', and a loose note in Ashby's hand naming the Cloakwood ford as the place 'to finish it'.
- Sister Maudra Kell at the Song of the Morning archive: the register of lost dawn-witness seals, Aubrey's question last autumn about how one is opened, and the folded pledge ticket he left with her for his widow.
- A forge apprentice at the Thunderhammer smithy: grumbling about night shifts for two hundred picks and forty sets of chain for 'a mine nobody owns'. The order book carries Ashby & Corve's mark and the Scornubel banker's name.
The next session's false lead: A tiefling in a road-dusty coat has been loitering at the top of Hesper's lane, and suspicion will fall on him as the watcher. The ordinary truth: he is waiting for the cooper next door, who owes him three days' wages for barrel hoops, and he is ashamed to knock again. The real watcher is the Red Sheaf stable lad, Wat Ferrow, who looks like nobody.
The hero's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): Bram has no magic and his chain mail cannot go quiet. If the party chooses to sneak into Thole's counting-room, someone has to keep Thole talking at the front for a quarter of an hour. A plain caravan guard come to pledge a shield is the one visitor Thole will believe and will haggle with at length. The price is that Bram has to hold a conversation he isn't built for while the others work. Thole's own desk holds a bill of lading that only a caravan guard would see is routed wrong.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): When Sefa comes near the dawn-witness seal, the light in her hands warms toward the wax, and the Lantern, in a voice like a lamp being lit, says only: 'It would open for you.' The temptation is to break a Morninglord oath-seal that was never hers and read a dead man's secrets, with the Lantern's price unspoken.
The act plan (yours alone; the player sees only the act number): about 4 hours, ~40 turns; the errand: Hesper Vallow pays fifty gold now and a hundred on delivery to recover her late husband's sealed iron coffer, unopened, from the moneylender Gaspar Thole before his pledge lapses at sundown and the coffer passes to a buyer called Corwen Ashby.
- act 1, to turn 6: Inside the shuttered house Hesper puts the errand in front of the three plainly: the coffer, Thole, sundown, Ashby, the pay, and the one condition that it stay shut. She does not say what she fears. They may question her, bargain, or walk away. (converge: Whatever they ask about leads to Thole's pledge, the deadline or the man in the lane: Hesper's husband, the watcher, the shutters, or what's in the coffer (she doesn't know).)
- act 2, to turn 20: The means are laid out and the fork appears. Thole's price has risen to three hundred gold because Ashby offered two hundred and fifty. The ticket clause with Sister Maudra offers a lawful redemption, but the temple will claim the coffer. Thole's strongroom offers theft. Ashby's departure at dark of (converge: The smithy, the inn, the temple and the lane each hold a person who knows one piece, and every piece points back to the coffer and to sundown: the apprentice and his picks, Wat Ferrow and his silver, Maudra and her ticket.)
- act 3, to turn 32: The chosen plan meets resistance in proportion to the stakes. Paying makes Thole tell Ashby who paid. The temple route costs the seal, and the coffer goes into temple keeping under Maudra's eye. Theft has the dawn-seal's danger and Thole's raised alarm. Force on the road means Ashby's blades and a c (converge: Any plan ends with the coffer in someone's hands at or before sundown. That makes the seal the next question: who can open it, and what will Hesper do.)
- act 4, to turn 40: The reckoning, where nothing is what it seems. The coffer goes to Hesper, to the temple, or to ash. The named hand is found or tried. Whatever it gives up shows that the caravans were routed, not robbed, and that a Fist captain's name is on the copies. The answer opens the larger question of who at  (converge: However the errand closes, the consequences point outward: the next caravan forming at Feldepost's, the cell's attention, and three seals still missing.)

Pell Dunmore: Coin, not favours. Favours are how the Guild kept me, and I paid my way out. I don't use the name I left with, and I don't like being asked twice. I watch hands, not faces. If this job starts to smell like Guild work, debts and silences and someone else's ledger, I want my pay and the door. Short sentences. I don't waste words on people who haven't earned them.

Sefa Marrin: The Lantern answered me in a dark ward, and I have never been told what I owe it. I heal because I can. I hate being looked at like a miracle, and worse like a sickness. With strangers I am gentle and a little formal. In a house of Lathander I keep my hands quiet. I want to be useful without being owned, by the light or by anyone.

Corwen Ashby: My name is Corwen Ashby this month. I buy iron and I buy pledges, and I am paid not to wonder what's in them. My orders are the coffer, unopened, on the Cloakwood road by dark. Who stands behind the man in Scornubel, I don't know and don't care to. Polite, unhurried, 'friend' to everyone, which means no one.

Hesper Vallow: Aubrey sealed contracts for twenty years and never told me what was in that coffer. He said only: keep it shut. Then he fell on the temple steps. A boy has stood at the top of my lane for three days. I speak in terms and clauses, and I pay exactly what I promise. I will not say my husband was afraid until I know what he was afraid of.

Gaspar Thole: A pledge is a pledge. At sundown the law is on my side. I don't like Ashby: he pays too much and smiles too little. But two hundred and fifty gold is two hundred and fifty gold. Give me a reason to refuse him that the town won't hang on me, and I might take it. I talk in sums and terms. I never say no outright. I sniff when a price offends me.

Maudra Kell: For ninety years the archive has listed four dawn-witness seals as lost to the fire, and I never believed the entry. Last autumn Aubrey Vallow asked me how such a seal is opened. I told him only the named hand. He left a folded paper with me for his widow. I am careful and dry, I quote the Morninglord's rule, and temple matters do not go into sellswords' pockets.

- The Zhentarim (the 'Ashby & Corve' cell): Keep the Way bleeding until the Council grants the toll right, then 'rescue' it. They are buying Aubrey's forfeited coffer through Thole so they can destroy it unopened, and they have a hired boy watching Hesper's lane in case she holds other copies.
- The Flaming Fist: Most of the Fist knows nothing; it is short of men and blames gnolls. Captain Halvard Roe sits on the toll question in the Gate, files reports that clear the cell, and takes their gold. If his name surfaces he will call it a Zhentarim forgery and send men to bury it.
- The Song of the Morning (temple of Lathander): The temple is Beregost's real authority and its court of contracts. Its archive has listed four dawn-witness seals as lost for ninety years. It wants them back quietly and would claim the coffer as temple property. It would also prefer that no one learn a temple healer was paid to overlook bruises on Aubrey's throat.
- The smiths of Beregost (Thunderhammer and the lesser forges): They are filling large advance-paid orders for mine-picks, chain and spearheads from Ashby & Corve. They suspect where the goods go and do not want to know. Their one aim is to keep the orders coming without being tied to the vanished caravans.
Secrets (not tied to a place):
- Aubrey Vallow did not die of the fall. The temple healer who laid him out saw finger-marks on his throat. A donation to the temple came the same week, and she wrote 'a fall'.
- Gaspar Thole's pledge book records the coffer as pledged by Aubrey eight months ago for one hundred and twenty gold, redeemable until sundown of this day. Aubrey paid him twenty gold more 'for silence and the full term'.
- Aubrey's pledge has a clause: the coffer may be redeemed by 'the bearer of my ticket or my lawful heir producing it'. The ticket is not in his papers. He left it, folded, with Sister Maudra Kell of the temple archive, 'for my widow, if it comes to it'.
- 'Ashby & Corve' has no house in Baldur's Gate and no letter of credit at the Counting House. Its notes are drawn on a banker in Scornubel, and that banker has no other clients on the Coast.
- At least three of the vanished caravans carried bills of lading sealed in Beregost and routed 'by the Cloakwood spur, for the ford'. No caravan master who knows the Way would take that road in that season.
- The Thunderhammer smithy's order book shows two hundred mine-picks and forty sets of shackle-chain paid in advance by Ashby & Corve. No mine near Beregost has admitted to buying them.
- Captain Halvard Roe of the Flaming Fist signed a report blaming 'gnoll bands' for the second caravan two days before anyone found the wagons.
- The boy watching Hesper's lane is Wat Ferrow, a stable lad at the Red Sheaf. Ashby pays him a silver a day to report who calls on her. He knows nothing beyond the coin and the description he was given.
- Thole is afraid of Ashby and would rather not sell to him. He will not refuse outright, but he would take any refusal that the town could not blame on him.

- clock_cell_attention: The cell notices who is working for Hesper Vallow (segments 6; when full: Ashby concludes Hesper has copies or hired help. Her house is broken into that night, and the party is named to the cell as a problem.)
- clock_next_caravan: A caravan forms at Feldepost's Inn with a bill of lading routed by the Cloakwood spur (segments 8; when full: The caravan leaves Beregost and vanishes on the Way, guards and all. A fourth set of empty wagons is left for the Fist to blame on gnolls.)
The wonder: The wax on Aubrey's iron coffer is pale gold and still faintly warm to the touch, and it is not his notary's mark. It shows a sun-disc split by an upright key, with a line of tiny dawn-script letters around the rim. Any light brought near it seems to lean toward it. Its history: It is one of four dawn-witness seals that the archivists of the Song of the Morning made about two centuries ago to witness oaths between merchant houses. A name is spoken into the wax as it is set. Only that hand can break it; any other hand makes the wax flare and burn the contents to ash. The archive has listed all four as lost in a fire ninety years ago. Aubrey had one, which means at least one was taken out before the fire, or by someone using it. The open question: Whose name did Aubrey speak into the wax? Hesper's, his own dead hand, or someone the party has not met? And where are the other three seals, and what are they witnessing now?
Clues to the truth:
- Thole's pledge book and counting-room, at his house on the main street: the coffer's entry, the sundown term, the twenty gold 'for silence', and a loose note in Ashby's hand naming the Cloakwood ford as the place 'to finish it'.
- Sister Maudra Kell at the Song of the Morning archive: the register of lost dawn-witness seals, Aubrey's question last autumn about how one is opened, and the folded pledge ticket he left with her for his widow.
- A forge apprentice at the Thunderhammer smithy: grumbling about night shifts for two hundred picks and forty sets of chain for 'a mine nobody owns'. The order book carries Ashby & Corve's mark and the Scornubel banker's name.
The next session's false lead: A tiefling in a road-dusty coat has been loitering at the top of Hesper's lane, and suspicion will fall on him as the watcher. The ordinary truth: he is waiting for the cooper next door, who owes him three days' wages for barrel hoops, and he is ashamed to knock again. The real watcher is the Red Sheaf stable lad, Wat Ferrow, who looks like nobody.
The hero's weakness tested (next session, for a reason, never a trap): Bram has no magic and his chain mail cannot go quiet. If the party chooses to sneak into Thole's counting-room, someone has to keep Thole talking at the front for a quarter of an hour. A plain caravan guard come to pledge a shield is the one visitor Thole will believe and will haggle with at length. The price is that Bram has to hold a conversation he isn't built for while the others work. Thole's own desk holds a bill of lading that only a caravan guard would see is routed wrong.
The patron's moment (at a temptation, not a comfort): When Sefa comes near the dawn-witness seal, the light in her hands warms toward the wax, and the Lantern, in a voice like a lamp being lit, says only: 'It would open for you.' The temptation is to break a Morninglord oath-seal that was never hers and read a dead man's secrets, with the Lantern's price unspoken.

- act 1, to turn 6: Inside the shuttered house Hesper puts the errand in front of the three plainly: the coffer, Thole, sundown, Ashby, the pay, and the one condition that it stay shut. She does not say what she fears. They may question her, bargain, or walk away. (converge: Whatever they ask about leads to Thole's pledge, the deadline or the man in the lane: Hesper's husband, the watcher, the shutters, or what's in the coffer (she doesn't know).)
- act 2, to turn 20: The means are laid out and the fork appears. Thole's price has risen to three hundred gold because Ashby offered two hundred and fifty. The ticket clause with Sister Maudra offers a lawful redemption, but the temple will claim the coffer. Thole's strongroom offers theft. Ashby's departure at dark of (converge: The smithy, the inn, the temple and the lane each hold a person who knows one piece, and every piece points back to the coffer and to sundown: the apprentice and his picks, Wat Ferrow and his silver, Maudra and her ticket.)
- act 3, to turn 32: The chosen plan meets resistance in proportion to the stakes. Paying makes Thole tell Ashby who paid. The temple route costs the seal, and the coffer goes into temple keeping under Maudra's eye. Theft has the dawn-seal's danger and Thole's raised alarm. Force on the road means Ashby's blades and a c (converge: Any plan ends with the coffer in someone's hands at or before sundown. I want to be useful without being owned, by the light or by anyone.
